title: Raising revenue right: Better taxes for development
gist: A World Bank report argues developing countries can raise more revenue while making taxes fairer and more efficient, because the problem is badly designed systems rather than low rates. It points to technology, transparency and trust, with Ethiopia, Argentina and Sierra Leone examples.

insights.claim: Tax revenues in many developing economies have barely budged in fifteen years even as spending needs and debt burdens have grown and development assistance has become less certain.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Fiscal squeeze on developing sovereigns will persist, raising pressure for domestic revenue reform.

insights.claim: Tax exemptions and loopholes cost developing-country governments roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of what they already collect.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Exemption reform is a large untapped revenue source without raising rates.

insights.claim: The report defines a fiscal frontier, the best combination of efficiency and fairness a country can achieve for a fixed revenue level given its economic structure, administrative capacity and informal sector size.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Use distance from the frontier to judge how much reform upside a country has.

insights.claim: The report challenges the assumption that efficiency and fairness always trade off, because most developing economies operate well below the frontier and can improve both by better design and collection.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Reform need not mean growth-for-equity trade-offs.
insights.quote: Raising Revenue Right challenges the idea that countries always face this trade-off.

insights.claim: The problem is rarely that tax rates are too low; it is that tax systems are riddled with poorly targeted exemptions, undermined by weak compliance and unable to track cross-border income and assets.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Base broadening and compliance, not rate hikes, are the lever to watch.
insights.locator: What's the best way to raise more tax revenue?

insights.claim: Commonly cited tax-to-GDP thresholds of 15-20 percent should be interpreted with caution, since governments can operate near the fiscal frontier at very different revenue levels.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Benchmarks based on tax-to-GDP thresholds may mislead sovereign assessments.

insights.claim: Electronic sales registration systems in Ethiopia increased value-added tax revenues by almost 50 percent, showing digital tools can yield quick gains even in low-capacity settings.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Tax-tech and e-invoicing vendors have a clear evidence base in low-capacity states.

insights.claim: Argentina's 2016 disclosure program, backed by the credible threat of automatic information exchange, uncovered hidden assets worth 21 percent of GDP and raised revenue equal to 1.8 percent of GDP.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: International tax transparency can unlock large offshore wealth for taxation.

insights.claim: In Sierra Leone, property tax payments rose when residents were shown concrete examples of public services financed by those revenues, so building trust is a revenue strategy.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Visible service delivery supports tax compliance.

insights.claim: Governments should begin with a diagnosis of how far the tax system is from its potential rather than a revenue target; highly indebted countries may prioritize low-cost extra revenue, while others may aim to collect the same amount more fairly.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Reform priorities will differ by debt position and financing access.

insights.claim: Where better public services far outweigh the costs of raising additional revenue, the case for collecting more is especially strong.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Spending quality conditions the case for higher taxes.
